overall:
Part 2: Each of the eight items has exactly one defensible response; I found no case where a second response would work as a natural reply. The traps match real Part 2 closely: wrong question type, repeated or similar-sounding words (sales/drive, train/trained, present/presenting), a tense mismatch, and 'Yes' to a WH question. Five of the eight keys are indirect answers, which fits the modern test. The scripts are short, natural and in the real register. The main gap is that nothing is hard. Every distractor can be ruled out on form (wrong question type or a recycled word), whereas the hardest real items include a distractor that is grammatical and on topic but doesn't actually respond. In my judgment the mix (3 easy, 5 medium, 0 hard) is on the easier side of a real set.

Part 3: All 12 questions have one answer supported by the transcript, and context makes the intended reading of both quoted phrases clear. Paraphrase between audio and keys is good (furniture and computers / office equipment, the price page / cost information, turn it over / check the underside), and the distractors use speaker-swap and recycled-word traps realistically. Conversation length, turn-taking and scenarios (office move, catering order, brochure proof, IT help desk) look like real Part 3. The weakest item is l-conv-03:0: the quoted line is nearly literal and its distractors are implausible, so it is easier than a real implied-meaning question. Compared with a real Part 3, this sample has no three-speaker conversation, no graphic question and nothing I would call hard, so it leans easy/medium (6 easy, 6 medium).

Part 4: All six questions are unambiguous. The two talks (a building-management announcement and a voicemail confirming a speaking engagement) are standard Part 4 genres of realistic length and density, and the question types (gist, reason, detail, listener identity, change, 'why does the speaker mention') are all real-test types. l-talk-01 uses British vocabulary (lifts, goods lift, half past eight) that the options paraphrase into American English. That is legitimate but slightly demanding. The maps-vs-reception trap in l-talk-01:2 and the send-vs-pick-up near miss in l-talk-02:2 are the most authentic distractors in the whole set. No question reaches hard (3 easy, 3 medium); a real set would add an implied-meaning or graphic question and one or two denser detail items.
